title: Wetland Removal Alters Hourly and Monthly Dynamics of In‐Stream Greenhouse Gas Production
content:
Abstract

Riverine wetlands are dynamic biogeochemical hotspots that significantly influence greenhouse gas (GHG) fluxes. In the context of widespread wetland loss, the response of in-stream GHG production remains poorly understood, largely due to the methodological challenge involved in disentangling local biogeochemical processes from upstream inputs and atmospheric exchange. To address this, we developed a Lagrangian-based mass-balance model and applied it to a riverine reach experiencing complete wetland removal. By employing two-station diel sampling combined with monthly campaigns, we quantified the net production rates of CO2, CH4, and N2O across both time scales before and after the perturbation. Our results reveal a fundamental shift triggered by wetland removal. On a diel scale, the strong, metabolically coupled patterns of GHG production observed during the wetland period were markedly attenuated, shifting the primary control from internal metabolism to external nutrient inputs. On a monthly scale, the reach transitioned from a periodic sink of N2O (as low as −3.63 μmol m−2 h−1) to a consistent source (monthly mean of 1.75 μmol m−2 h−1). Conversely, the production of CH4 and CO2 decreased substantially by 60% and 20%, respectively, with the reach periodically becoming a net CH4 sink post-removal. This study demonstrates the power of the Lagrangian approach for resolving reach-scale GHG production and provides a clear example of how wetland removal can alter diel and monthly riverine GHG emissions.
